Documentation → Administration → Certificate Manager

Certificate Manager

Issue, import, deploy, rotate and revoke certificates on FortiWeb and FortiADC appliances through ADCS or ACME, and keep the fleet clean with a lifecycle policy.

👤 ForAdministrator
🔑 Permissionsusers.manage
📍 WhereGlobal ADOM → Automation → Certificate Manager, or in the FortiWeb / FortiADC ADOM → Operations → Automation → Certificate Manager (URL /cert-manager/) · configuration in Settings → Certificates & Trust → Certificate Manager

What is it?#

The Certificate Manager runs the whole life of a CA-signed certificate on your appliances: SATOM generates the key and CSR, has your CA sign it (Microsoft ADCS or any ACME CA such as Let's Encrypt), uploads certificate and key to the device, and later swaps, renews and revokes it. It also shows every certificate already on your FortiWeb and FortiADC boxes, with expiry and where each one is bound.

ℹ️Note — Three different certificate questions

This page is about certificates on the appliances. The certificate SATOM itself presents to your browser is Node TLS. The CAs SATOM trusts when it connects to an appliance are the trust store.

What does it do?#

  • Managed certificates — an inventory of the certificates SATOM issued: device, class, SANs, expiry, days left, status and bound policies, with a per-certificate timeline.
  • On-device certificates — a cached, de-duplicated view of the certificate stores on every FortiWeb and FortiADC (Local, SNI, CA, Let's Encrypt on FortiWeb; Local, CA, Intermediate CA, Remote on FortiADC). The same certificate on several boxes is shown once, with every device it lives on.
  • Issuance through a pluggable protocol: ADCS / enterprise CA (a command template, certipy by default) or ACME (RFC 8555, generated lego commands by default). The protocol is a setting, not a code change.
  • Deploy — FortiWeb receives certificate and key over SSH; FortiADC over a REST upload. The new certificate is uploaded under a new, date-stamped name and is not bound to anything.
  • Swap — point a server policy, an SNI member or the device GUI/admin HTTPS certificate at a certificate.
  • Three origins — signed by the configured CA, a CSR for another CA (SATOM keeps the key; you import the signed certificate), or a certificate and key imported from outside (PEM or PKCS#12).
  • Staged rotation — a renewal is deployed before expiry and takes over the bindings on its swap date; the old certificate stays on the device for a one-click roll back, then leaves the device and later SATOM, each after the number of days you set.
  • Revoke with whichever CA is configured, recorded in the revocation register (pending at the CA when SATOM cannot revoke it itself) — refused while the certificate is still in use unless you confirm it.
  • Lifecycle policy — default rotation windows, and removal of revoked or expired material from devices, manually or from a scheduled action.
  • Renewals page — the renewal journal of every SATOM node plus every failed sign, deploy, swap, renew or revoke event on a managed certificate, with the exact error text.
  1. 1Generatekey + CSR built in SATOM; key stored encrypted
  2. 2Signthe active protocol's submit command
  3. 3Storeserial, validity and SANs parsed from the signed cert
  4. 4Deployupload under a new date-stamped name (SSH or REST)
  5. 5Swapa renewal takes over the bindings on its swap date
  6. 6Retireoff the device, then out of SATOM; revoked as it leaves if the policy says so

Requirements#

  • The appliances are registered in SATOM (see Appliances). FortiWeb deployment uses SSH with the appliance's stored credentials; FortiADC uses its REST API.
  • For ADCS: the CA host, CA name and enrolment user in Settings, and an ADCS template on every certificate class you issue in. The signing binary (certipy by default) must be installed on the SATOM node.
  • For ACME: a directory URL, the CA's Terms of Service accepted, and a validation method that can actually reach this node (webroot path, port, or a DNS provider with its credentials). The SATOM installer places the lego client and the output helper script. The classes' ADCS template field is not used.
  • Optional: e-mail configured in Settings if you fill Notify emails (lifecycle events).

Permissions#

Every Certificate Manager page and action, and the Certificate Manager settings tab, requires users.manage — in practice the Administrator profile. The routes check the legacy user_manage key, which is derived from users.manage.

  • The Certificate Manager entry (Global ADOM → Automation), its tile on the Global home and its buttons are shown only to holders of users.manage; anyone else who opens the address directly gets 403 Forbidden. The Automation group itself needs write access. Every device ADOM draws the entry under Operations › Automation: live in FortiWeb and FortiADC, where the page lists only that ADOM's devices, and greyed out with the reason in FortiGate, FortiAnalyzer and FortiAuthenticator, whose certificates SATOM does not manage.
  • The Certificates & Trust group of Settings is only offered to administrators.

See Permissions for the full list.

ℹ️Note

Changed in 2.11.0: ACME issuance no longer requires an ADCS template on the class, the pages name the configured protocol and the target appliance, the ADCS request id is recorded for revocation, and the Certificate Manager menu entry is shown only to holders of users.manage.

ℹ️Note

Changed in 3.1.0: the Certificate Manager menu entry moved from the Global group to Automation in the Global ADOM.

ℹ️Note

Changed on 2026-10-15: Generate CSR creates a request for another CA and Import brings in a certificate and its key. Renewals are staged with per-certificate windows and can be rolled back. Revocation works with any configured CA and is recorded in the revocation register. Every row has its action buttons, and a certificate in use cannot be deleted.

ℹ️Note

Changed on 2026-10-14: every device ADOM shows Certificate Manager under Operations › Automation (live in FortiWeb and FortiADC, greyed out elsewhere). In the Global ADOM, Scan devices now scans only FortiWeb and FortiADC appliances. It used to send FortiWeb requests to FortiGate, FortiAnalyzer and FortiAuthenticator and then list them as unreachable.

How to use#

Choose and configure the issuance protocol#

  1. Open Settings → Certificates & Trust → Certificate Manager (or click Policy on the Certificate Manager page).
  2. In Issuance protocol (CA backend), pick the Active protocol: ADCS / enterprise CA (command template — certipy, certreq…) or ACME (RFC 8555 — certbot, acme.sh, lego…).
  3. Fill the card for that protocol (tables under Configuration), the per-class cards and the Lifecycle policy card.
  4. Click Save Settings. The flash Certificate Manager settings saved. confirms it.

Everything on this tab is one form except the DNS provider cards, which save on their own.

Configure ACME#

  1. Set Client to lego (recommended — one static binary, ~150 DNS providers) unless you need another client.
  2. Pick a Directory URL from the suggestions. Use a staging directory (for example Let's Encrypt — staging (test first!)) until one issuance works end to end.
  3. Enter the Account email, keep the Account key directory, tick I accept the CA's Terms of Service, and add EAB values if your CA needs them (ZeroSSL, Google Trust Services, private CAs).
  4. In ACME — domain validation, choose the Challenge: - http-01 — web authentication: keep Mode = webroot — the local web server keeps :80 and the Webroot path. - dns-01 — DNS provider (wildcards, no inbound port): pick the Provider, and set Resolvers to a public resolver if your internal DNS shadows the zone. - tls-alpn-01 — TLS on :443.
  5. Leave Command source on Generated from the fields above (recommended). The submit and revoke commands are regenerated every time you save.
  6. Save Settings.

⚠️Warning — Custom commands

Custom — I write the commands runs your command with the privileges of the SATOM service. It is audited and secrets are redacted from the logs, but treat it as remote code execution.

Enter DNS provider credentials (dns-01)#

  1. Below the main form, open the provider in DNS provider credentials (dns-01). A missing: … badge lists required variables that have no value yet.
  2. Fill the fields and click Save credentials. Secret fields show •••••• (unchanged) once stored; leaving them blank keeps the stored value, and the Clear tick erases it.
  3. To support a DNS service that is not listed, use Add or edit a DNS provider: a Slug, Label, Flag (the value passed to lego --dns, or exec with an EXEC_PATH field for a hook script), Docs URL, the Fields JSON list, Sort and Enabled, then Save provider. Using an existing slug edits that entry.

Sign with a CA held in an OPNsense firewall#

SATOM ships a signer for the ADCS command template that has a CA in an OPNsense firewall (System › Trust) sign the request.

  1. On the firewall, create a user with only the System: Certificate Manager privilege and give it an API key. Note the refid of the issuing CA (System › Trust › Authorities).
  2. On the SATOM node, print the firewall's public-key pin: /opt/satom/venv/bin/python /opt/satom/scripts/opnsense_ca_signer.py pin --url https://<firewall>:<port>. Compare it with the firewall's certificate before you use it.
  3. In Settings → Certificate Manager, keep the protocol on ADCS / enterprise CA. Set CA to https://<firewall>:<port>, CA name to the refid, User to the API key, and the API secret in the password box.
  4. On each class, set ADCS template to the OPNsense certificate type (server_cert, combined_server_client or usr_cert) and Signing command to: /opt/satom/venv/bin/python /opt/satom/scripts/opnsense_ca_signer.py sign --url {ca} --ca-ref {ca_name} --key {user} --cert-type {template} --csr {csr} --out {out} --pin-sha256 <pin>

ℹ️Note

The private key never leaves SATOM; the firewall receives the CSR only. OPNsense drops a request's subject alternative names when it signs, so the signer sends them separately. The signer checks the pin before it sends any credential, and it refuses a secret on its command line. It reads the secret from $SATOM_CA_SECRET, which the Certificate Manager sets for every ADCS signing and revoke command. The signer has no revoke command, so a revocation is recorded in the revocation register as pending at the CA until you revoke it in the firewall and confirm it.

Choose the certificate provider#

Certificate Manager → Providers lists the providers the person issuing a certificate picks from — seeded with Class E (the internal CA, internal only) and Class C (another provider). Each has a name, the protocol it is reached with (configured = the one in Settings, or ADCS / ACME) and Internal only: its certificates may serve Internal server policies only (the Plugin Studio certificate step refuses any other zone). A certificate remembers its provider, so its renewal and its revocation go back to the same one. Nothing is derived from the domain name: the provider is the user's choice. The list cannot be emptied.

Issue a new certificate#

  1. Open Certificate Manager and click New Certificate. The first tab, Signed by the configured CA, is the one described here; it is disabled until the active protocol is configured.
  2. Choose the Target appliance (FortiWeb or FortiADC), the Provider, the Certificate class, the CN / hostname and optional Extra SANs (optional) (comma separated; a bare name is a DNS name, IP: marks an address).
  3. Keep Deploy to the appliance after signing (FortiWeb: cert + key over SSH; FortiADC: REST upload) ticked to upload it straight away.

The page names the active protocol (ACME or ADCS) and, when it is not configured yet, points to the settings that are missing. 4. Optionally open Renewal & rotation to set this certificate's windows (empty = the defaults). 5. Click Generate, sign and deploy. On success you land on the certificate's detail page.

The certificate is not bound to any policy yet — swap it in during a maintenance window.

Generate a CSR for another CA and import the signed certificate#

  1. Click Generate CSR (or the CSR for another CA tab of New Certificate), choose the appliance, class, CN and SANs, and click Generate key + CSR.
  2. The certificate's page opens in status awaiting signature with Waiting for the signature of another CA: - 1. Download the CSR and have it signed — Download CSR saves <name>.csr; Copy puts it on the clipboard. - 2. Import the signed certificate — paste or upload the PEM the CA returned (the chain may follow the leaf), keep Deploy to the device after the import ticked, and click Import certificate.
  3. SATOM accepts it only if its public key is the stored key, every requested SAN is present and it has not expired. A pasted private key or a PKCS#12 is refused here: the key of the request was made in SATOM and never leaves it.

The private key is generated and kept encrypted in SATOM; only the CSR goes to the other CA.

Import a certificate and key made outside SATOM#

Click Import (or the Import certificate + key tab), choose the appliance and class, then paste the PEM certificate and its key, or upload a PKCS#12 (.p12/.pfx) with its password, and click Import. The key is stored encrypted and the certificate is marked key from outside. To replace an existing certificate with one made outside, use Replace with a certificate + key made outside SATOM on its page instead; it then rotates like a renewal.

Swap a certificate into use#

  • Managed certificate: on its detail page, under Swap binding (immediate), pick the Server policy and click Swap now. The certificate becomes active and the certificate it replaced becomes superseded. The button is disabled when no policy could be read or no private key is stored.
  • Any on-device certificate: in On-device certificates, click the eye icon, then in Swap onto this cert choose Server policy (primary certificate), SNI member or GUI / admin cert, the target, and click Swap.

For a planned change, schedule the swap through a change request instead.

Renew a managed certificate#

A renewal never replaces a certificate in place, so issuing and switching never cut connections at the same moment:

  1. Renew — N days before expiry (or with Renew now / Generate a new CSR now), the replacement is issued and deployed under a new name, status staged.
  2. Swap — on its swap date (N days later), every binding of the old certificate moves to the new one. Swap now does it immediately.
  3. Roll back — while the old one is still on the device, Roll back to returns every binding to it.
  4. Off the device — N days after the swap the old certificate is removed from the device (refused while anything still uses it), and revoked with reason superseded if the policy says so.
  5. Out of SATOM — N days later its private key is purged; serial, dates and timeline stay under Archived certificates.

The four windows come from Settings → Lifecycle policy and can be changed per certificate on its page (Change the windows of this certificate). The swap delay must be shorter than the renew window, so the swap lands before the old certificate expires.

With Renew automatically on, the sweep starts the renewal itself: signed and deployed for the configured CA. For another CA it generates a new CSR and notifies you, and the swap is scheduled when you import the signed certificate. Imported certificates are only notified: renew them outside SATOM and use Replace.

Revoke, remove or forget a certificate#

  • Revoke (row button or detail page, with a confirmation) runs the revoke command of the configured CA, with a reason. When SATOM cannot revoke it (the CA has no revoke command, or another CA signed it), the certificate is marked revoked and the Revocation register shows it pending at the CA until you click Mark revoked at the CA. A certificate still in use is refused unless you tick Revoke even though it is in use (a compromised key). Tick Also remove it from the device to delete it from the box too.
  • Revocation register — every revocation with serial, reason, CA, result and who; it stays after the certificate record is deleted.
  • Remove from device (on-device detail) is offered only on a device where the certificate is bound to nothing.
  • Delete record asks for confirmation and is refused while the certificate is bound, or when its bindings cannot be read. Tick Revoke it first and/or Remove it from the device too; if either fails, nothing is deleted. Otherwise the device copy is not touched.

Scan devices and run the lifecycle sweep#

  1. Click Scan devices to read every appliance's certificate stores and refresh the cache (expiry, issuer, SANs, bindings). Until the first scan the table shows a live read with names only.
  2. The Lifecycle — due for revocation / device cleanup card lists revoke due, delete due and blocked certificates. Click Run sweep now to apply the policy immediately.

Check renewals#

Click Renewals to see, per SATOM node, the current service certificate, its renewal strategy and the journal of every attempt, plus Appliance certificates — failed lifecycle events. Run renewal pass now runs the nightly renewal pass of the node certificate on this node (see Node TLS).

Configuration#

ADCS connection (Linux enrolment client)

Field Description Required Example
Signing binary {bin} Enrolment client Yes (defaults to certipy) certipy
CA host / config {ca} CA or DC host / config string Yes pki.example.com
CA name {ca_name} Name of the CA Yes EXAMPLE-CA
Domain {domain} Domain of the enrolment account Usually example.com
Enrolment user {user} Enrolment account Yes svc-enroll
Password {password} (encrypted) Stored encrypted; blank keeps the stored one; Clear stored password erases it Usually —
Name date format {date} strftime format used in certificate names No (default %Y%m%d) %Y%m%d
Notify emails (lifecycle events) Recipients for "Certificate ready", "Certificate revoked" and sweep results No pki-team@example.com

Per class — one card each for Server (Server Authentication), Client+Server (both EKU) and Client (Client Authentication):

Field Description Required Example
ADCS template {template} CA template name; must be non-empty for the class to issue under ADCS. Not used under ACME. ADCS only WebServer
Key type RSA or EC (P-256) Yes RSA
Key size RSA bits (minimum 2048 is enforced) Yes 2048
Renew before (days) Window used by the scheduled renew actions No (default 30) 30
Subject format DN built from {cn} No (default CN={cn}) CN={cn},O=Example
SAN format SANs built from {cn} No (default DNS:{cn}) DNS:{cn}
Signing command (submit) / Revoke command ADCS command templates; tokens {bin} {user} {domain} {password} {ca} {ca_name} {template} {csr} {out} {serial} {request_id}. The password is also in the command's environment as $SATOM_CA_SECRET, so a template can leave {password} out of the command line Yes for ADCS default certipy req … / certipy ca … -revoke

ACME

Field Description Required Example
Client lego or other (write the commands yourself) Yes lego
Client binary {bin} / Output helper {helper} Client and the shipped helper that copies the issued cert to the path the pipeline expects Yes lego
Directory URL {directory} ACME directory; suggestions for Let's Encrypt, Buypass, ZeroSSL, Google Trust Services Yes Let's Encrypt staging
Account email {email} Registration e-mail Recommended pki@example.com
Account key directory {acme_path} Must persist (rate limits, revocation of earlier certs) Yes (default under the data directory) —
Key type {key_type} EC256, EC384, RSA2048, RSA3072, RSA4096 Yes EC256
I accept the CA's Terms of Service Needed for the generated commands to count as configured Yes ticked
EAB key id / EAB HMAC key External Account Binding; the HMAC is stored encrypted CA-dependent —
Challenge http-01, dns-01, tls-alpn-01 Yes http-01
Mode / Webroot path / Port http-01: webroot (default /var/www/acme) or standalone; port for standalone and tls-alpn Per challenge webroot
Provider / Resolvers / Propagation wait (s) / Skip propagation check dns-01 settings Per challenge 1.1.1.1:53
Command source / Signing command / Revoke command Generated (default) or custom Yes Generated

Lifecycle policy — rotation windows & device cleanup (defaults; each certificate can override them)

Field Description Default
Swap (days after the renewal) When a renewal takes over the bindings; must be shorter than the class's renew window 3
Old cert off the device (days after the swap) The old certificate stays for a roll back until then 14
Kept in SATOM (days after it left the device) Then its private key is purged; the record stays 30
Revoke the old cert when it leaves the device Reason superseded on
Delete expired from device after (days) Days after expiry 30
Delete revoked certs from devices (once unbound) Remove revoked material on
Auto-apply When off, the scheduled sweep only reports; Run sweep now always applies off

Example#

🧪Example — Let's Encrypt certificate for a FortiWeb virtual server

  1. Settings → Certificate Manager: Active protocol = ACME, Directory URL = Let's Encrypt staging, account email, ToS accepted, Challenge = dns-01, provider selected and its credentials saved. Save Settings.
  2. Certificate Manager → New Certificate: target fweb-01, class Server, CN shop.example.com, Extra SANs www.example.com. Generate, Sign & Deploy.
  3. The detail page shows pending, the timeline shows generate, sign, deploy. In the maintenance window, choose server policy shop-https and Swap now — the status becomes active.
  4. Once staging works, switch the directory to production and issue again.

Result#

  • A managed certificate row with status awaiting signature (CSR for another CA), pending (signed or imported, and deployed if chosen), staged (a renewal waiting for its swap date), active, superseded once its renewal took over, or revoked. How close a certificate is to expiry shows next to Expires, and Next step says what happens next and when.
  • Under ADCS, the request id the signer prints (for example Request ID is 42) is stored with the certificate and passed to the revoke command as {request_id}.
  • Each step writes a timeline event (generate, sign, import, deploy, schedule, swap, rollback, renew, remove, revoke, archive, lifecycle, error) and an audit log entry named certmgr.<step>. Settings changes are audited as settings.cert_manager, settings.acme_provider_creds, settings.acme_provider and settings.acme_provider_delete — credential values are never logged.
  • Failed events appear on the Renewals page.
  • With Notify emails set, SATOM mails [Cert Manager] Certificate ready, [Cert Manager] Certificate revoked and [Cert Manager] Lifecycle sweep.

Troubleshooting#

"Certificate creation failed: class 'server' has no ADCS template configured (Settings → Certificate Manager)."#

Possible causes - The active protocol is ADCS and the class's ADCS template field is empty. (Under ACME the field is not checked.)

Solution 1. Settings → Certificate Manager → the class card → enter your ADCS template name in ADCS template. 2. Save Settings and issue again.

Verification — the new certificate's timeline shows a generate and a sign event.

"signing binary not found" / "signer produced no certificate (rc=…)"#

Possible causes - {bin} points to a client that is not installed on this node. - The CA refused the request (wrong template, credentials, challenge failure); the message ends with the redacted command output.

Solution 1. Read the error event on the certificate's timeline or on Renewals; secrets are shown as ********. 2. For ACME, test on a staging directory; check the webroot is served on port 80 or the DNS credentials are correct. 3. satom diagnose acme on the node checks the client, account key, webroot and provider credentials.

Verification — a new issuance records a sign event with the serial and expiry.

"DNS provider '…' is missing required credentials: …"#

Possible causes — a required variable of the selected provider has no stored value.

Solution — open the provider in DNS provider credentials (dns-01), fill the fields named in the missing: badge, Save credentials.

Verification — the missing: badge disappears.

"signing command timed out after 180s"#

Possible causes — the client waited too long (DNS propagation through an internal resolver, an unreachable CA).

Solution — set Resolvers to a public resolver, lower Propagation wait (s), or check outbound access to the CA.

"Certificate creation failed: signed but deploy failed: …"#

Possible causes — SSH (FortiWeb) or REST (FortiADC) to the appliance failed, or the generated name is not valid on the device (letters, digits, ., -, _, at most 63 characters).

Solution — fix connectivity or credentials on the appliance record; the certificate is signed and kept, so open its detail page and use Renew now to issue and deploy again.

"Revoked at the CA, but NOT deleted from the device — still bound to: …"#

Possible causes — the certificate is still used by a server policy, SNI member or the GUI.

Solution — swap the bindings to another certificate, then remove it from the on-device detail page or let the lifecycle sweep delete it.

"Not removed: could not fully verify bindings (a device read failed); refusing to remove"#

Possible causes — one of the binding reads (server policies, SNI, global settings) failed, so SATOM cannot prove the certificate is unused. Removal fails closed.

Solution — check the appliance is reachable and retry.

"Built-in providers cannot be deleted — disable them instead."#

Shipped providers are re-seeded at boot, so they can only be disabled: open Add or edit a DNS provider, enter the same slug, untick Enabled, Save provider.

The lifecycle card shows "blocked"#

A certificate is due for revocation or deletion but is still bound in SATOM's records. Swap the binding first; the sweep also re-checks bindings live and skips anything it cannot prove unbound.

Advanced#

Advanced Secrets, environment and redaction
  • Private keys are generated in SATOM and stored Fernet-encrypted on the certificate record. The ADCS password, the EAB HMAC key and every DNS-provider field marked secret are stored encrypted and never returned to the browser.
  • The signer runs with a minimal environment: a fixed passthrough (PATH, locale, TZ, CA-bundle and proxy variables) plus the provider's variables. DNS credentials travel only in that environment, never in the command line. HOME is the provider's ACME account directory when one is set, otherwise the private temporary directory created for that call — never a shared directory such as /tmp, because a signer keeps state (account keys, configuration) under HOME.
  • Command templates are split into arguments before tokens are substituted, so a value with spaces stays one argument. Every secret is masked from the stored output.
Advanced Generated lego commands

With Client = lego and Command source = generated, the submit command is {helper} {out} {bin} run --accept-tos plus --email, --server, --path, EAB flags when set, --key-type, the challenge flags (--dns {dns_flag} with optional --dns.resolvers, --dns.propagation.wait, --dns.propagation.disable-ans; or --tls --tls.address :{http_port}; or --http --http.webroot {webroot} / --http.address :{http_port}) and --csr {csr}. Revocation is {bin} certificates revoke … --cert.name {cn} --reason 4 (superseded).

Advanced DNS provider catalog

The catalog is a database table seeded insert-only at boot from the shipped provider list; rows you add or edit are never overwritten, and only rows you added can be deleted. A provider's form is rendered from its field list (env, label, secret, required, help, default).

Advanced Scheduled actions

On Settings → System → System Automations: Cert Manager — scan device certificates (cert_scan, intended daily). On Automation → Automations, where operators can schedule them: Cert Manager — renew Server certs / Client+Server certs / Client certs (renew managed certificates within the class's Renew before (days), deploy under a new name, never swap; also offered as change-request types), and Cert Manager — lifecycle sweep (revoke + cleanup) (report-only unless Auto-apply is on; when scheduled it runs only bound to an approved change request, inside its window). Each needs target devices. See Scheduled actions.

Advanced Scope and limits
  • The pages follow the active ADOM: a concrete ADOM shows its own appliances and their certificates; Global shows all. Managed certificates without a device show everywhere.
  • The managed-certificate Swap now sets a FortiWeb server policy's certificate field; SNI and GUI swaps are on the on-device detail page.
  • The Renewals JSON at /cert-manager/renewals/durability.json (?force=1 bypasses the pull throttle) reports how much renewal history each node has archived.
